title: Supply-Chain Security for Open-Source Dependencies
content:
An open-source library arrives with more than its source code. Its release artifact, indirect dependencies, build process, maintainer account, and update path all become part of your application’s risk. Supply-chain security starts with knowing what entered the project and how it reached production. A vulnerability scanner helps, but it cannot establish who built an artifact or whether every dependency is necessary.

Build an inventory you can explain

Start with manifests and lock files. Record direct packages, resolved versions, package sources, and the transitive packages they bring in. GitHub's dependency-graph documentation explains how manifests, lock files, and submitted dependency data support a repository inventory. Coverage varies by ecosystem and what the repository supplies, so compare the graph with the actual production build. A dependency not visible to one scanner may still ship in an image or bundle.

Assign an owner to each direct dependency. Ask what feature requires it, whether a platform or existing library already covers the job, and how it is updated. A package with a narrow purpose can be easier to review than a broad convenience dependency, but package count alone is not a security score. Removing a dependency may introduce custom code with its own maintenance cost. Record the tradeoff rather than treating “fewer packages” as an automatic answer.

Pin versions through the package manager's normal lock mechanism and use reproducible installation commands in CI. Review changes to the lock file when a manifest changes. A one-line direct upgrade can refresh many transitive packages. The lock file gives you a snapshot, not assurance that each package is trustworthy. Keep the installation source explicit so a similarly named package from a different registry does not slip into the build.

Review the change before it lands

GitHub describes dependency review as a pull-request view of added, removed, and updated packages, including indirect changes and known vulnerability information. Use it to ask why a new package appears and whether an update has a safer version. A known-vulnerability database cannot contain every exploit or malicious release; a clean result is useful evidence, not proof of safety.

Check the project's official release history, documentation, license, and maintenance path. Verify that the package you intend to use is the one maintained by the expected project. Pay attention to unexpected maintainer or repository changes, unusual install scripts, and sudden large dependency changes. These are review triggers rather than verdicts. A project can legitimately change maintainers or packaging; investigate the reason before accepting the update.

Separate source provenance from artifact provenance. The repository you inspect may differ from the package archive installed in CI. SLSA 1.2 describes tracks and levels for improving source and build supply-chain guarantees, including provenance. A signed statement or provenance record is valuable only when your process verifies its identity and ties it to the artifact you actually consume. Do not claim SLSA compliance from a badge without checking the relevant level and evidence.

Control the build and the update path

Use a trusted CI environment with scoped credentials. Dependency installation can run scripts, so avoid giving a pull request from an untrusted contributor access to production secrets. Keep publish tokens separate from ordinary test jobs. Record which source commit, workflow, and dependency snapshot produced the release artifact. If the build system supports attestations, verify them at the consumption boundary rather than merely generating files that nobody reads.

Set an update cadence. Security advisories require prompt triage, but routine updates also prevent a large jump from accumulating. Test new versions against behavior that matters to your app, not just installation success. If a fix requires a breaking major upgrade, record a temporary mitigation and an owner for the migration. If a package is unmaintained, evaluate replacement or isolation rather than leaving an alert permanently open.

When an incident affects a dependency, answer four questions: Is the package present in the shipped artifact? Which version? Is the vulnerable code path reachable in this use? What safe replacement or mitigation is available? A dependency graph narrows the search, but runtime configuration and build output determine exposure. Keep a record of the conclusion and evidence, including uncertainty. Avoid announcing that a product is unaffected solely because one scanner did not alert.

Hypothetical example: a small CSV parser

Imagine a hypothetical team adding a CSV parser for a single import screen. The direct package appears small, but the lock-file diff adds an archive utility and a post-install script through a transitive dependency. A reviewer checks whether the parser needs that feature, verifies the package's official repository and license, and tests a safer version that avoids the extra utility. The team also runs malformed-file tests because the parser handles untrusted uploads.

Suppose the project keeps the package after review. The decision note records the exact version, registry, reason for use, update owner, and tests. This is an illustrative process, not a claim about any real parser. It shows why the relevant question is not simply “does the scanner pass?” but “what entered our application, through which route, and with what evidence?”

Checklist for a dependency pull request

  • State the feature that requires the direct package.
  • Review the full manifest and lock-file diff, including transitive changes.
  • Confirm the official package source, license, and maintenance signals.
  • Check advisories and document the limits of scanner coverage.
  • Run relevant tests on the resolved version in controlled CI.
  • Record build and artifact provenance where available.
  • Assign an owner for updates, incident triage, and eventual removal.

Supply-chain security is continuous. The strongest small-team practice is an inventory that matches the shipped product, a review that explains each addition, a build path with bounded authority, and a way to respond when new information appears. Each layer makes a future incident easier to scope without pretending risk can be reduced to one badge.
excerpt: Protect an application’s dependency chain with a real inventory, reviewed lock-file changes, controlled builds, artifact provenance, and ongoing update ownership.
